Transubstantiation
TRAN-sub-stan-she-AY-shun
noun (Roman Catholic doctrine)
From Latin trans (across) and substantia (substance), coined to name a supposed change of underlying being; defined dogmatically at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and Trent (1551).

Biblical Definition

Transubstantiation is the Roman dogma that, at the priest's consecration, the whole substance of the bread is changed into the substance of Christ's body and the whole substance of the wine into His blood, the outward appearances alone remaining. Scripture will not bear this weight. When our Lord said “This is my body,” He spoke as He often did in figure—“I am the door,” “I am the vine”—and He stood bodily before the disciples, holding bread in His hand, plainly distinct from it. The dogma collides head-on with the finished work of Calvary, for the priest claims to offer Christ afresh as a propitiatory sacrifice, whereas Hebrews testifies that by one offering He hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified. A sacrifice repeated is a sacrifice unfinished; but our great High Priest sat down, His work complete. The Reformed faith confesses instead a true spiritual presence: in the Supper the believer, by faith and through the Holy Spirit, feeds really upon the crucified and risen Christ, not by any carnal grinding with the teeth but by the soul's laying hold of Him. The elements remain bread and wine, signs and seals of the covenant. To bow before the consecrated host is therefore idolatry, worshipping a creature in place of the Creator. We hold fast the apostolic ordinance: do this in remembrance of Me.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Roman doctrine that the bread and wine of the Mass are converted in substance into the actual body and blood of Christ.

TRANSUBSTANTIATION, noun [Latin trans, across, and substantia, substance.] In the Roman church, the supposed conversion of the whole substance of the bread and wine in the eucharist into the body and blood of Christ, the accidents alone remaining.

A doctrine defined at the Lateran Council of 1215 and anathematized against by the Reformed churches.

Distinguished from the Lutheran consubstantiation and from the Reformed confession of a spiritual presence received by faith.

The ground of the Roman Mass, condemned as a renewed offering of Christ contrary to Scripture.

“For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.” Hebrews 10:14.

Key Scripture

Heb 10:14 — "For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified."

Joh 19:30 — "When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost."

1Co 11:24 — "And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me."

Heb 10:12 — "But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God;"

Modern Corruption

Rome corrupts the Supper by teaching that the substance of bread and wine literally becomes Christ's flesh and blood, making the Mass a repeated propitiatory sacrifice and the host an object of worship.

expand to see more

The Roman doctrine of transubstantiation, fixed at Lateran IV and Trent, holds that after consecration nothing of bread and wine remains but their accidents, the substance having been changed into Christ's very body and blood. From this follows the adoration of the host and the sacrifice of the Mass. Scripture refutes both. Hebrews insists that Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for ever and then sat down; a finished work cannot be repeated upon ten thousand altars. To re-present Him as a sin-offering is to deny that “It is finished” meant what it said.

Against the carnal eating Rome demands, the Reformed faith confesses that believers feed upon Christ truly but spiritually, by faith and through the Spirit, while the elements remain bread and wine—signs and seals, not the thing signified. To bend the knee before a wafer is idolatry, ascribing to a creature the worship due God alone. We recover the plain words of institution: “this do in remembrance of me,” a memorial and communion, not a sacrifice and not a transmutation.

Hebrew Roots

The root joins Latin trans, across, to substantia, the underlying being of a thing.

expand to see more

trans — Latin, across, over, beyond.

substantia — Latin, that which stands under; underlying essence.

Combined to assert a change of essence beneath unchanged appearances.

A scholastic category imported to defend the Mass, not drawn from Scripture.

The Reformed answer keeps substance and sign distinct, joined only sacramentally.

Usage

"The Reformer preached against transubstantiation, showing from Hebrews that one offering had perfected the saints for ever."

"Because transubstantiation makes the Mass a renewed sacrifice, it overthrows the sufficiency of the cross."

"Where Rome adores the host, the Reformed believer lifts his heart to the Christ enthroned above, feeding on Him by faith."
